claim: Eight mouse strains (129S1/SvImJ, A/J, C57BL/6, CAST/EiJ, NOD/ShiLtJ, NZO/HILtJ, PWK/PhJ, WSB/EiJ) collectively span 90% of the mouse genetic diversity commonly used in laboratory experiments.
source: Among eight strains of inbred laboratory mice (129S1/SvImJ, A/J, C57BL/6, CAST/EiJ, NOD/ShiLtJ, NZO/HILtJ, PWK/PhJ, WSB/EiJ) that collectively span 90% of the mouse genetic diversity commonly used in laboratory experiments (Roberts et al., 2007), survival from malaria infection ranges from less than 5–100% (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roberts et al., 2007, which provides the basis for the genetic diversity estimate.

claim: Survival from malaria infection in eight mouse strains ranges from less than 5% to 100%.
source: Among eight strains of inbred laboratory mice (129S1/SvImJ, A/J, C57BL/6, CAST/EiJ, NOD/ShiLtJ, NZO/HILtJ, PWK/PhJ, WSB/EiJ) that collectively span 90% of the mouse genetic diversity commonly used in laboratory experiments (Roberts et al., 2007), survival from malaria infection ranges from less than 5–100% (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1, which displays survival data across the eight mouse strains.

claim: Host genetics is a major determinant of variation in resilience to malaria.
source: While it is difficult to disentangle the factors contributing to this variation in resilience to malaria, host genetics is a major determinant (Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2005; López et al., 2010; Hedrick, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2005; López et al., 2010; Hedrick, 2011) that establish host genetics as a major determinant.

claim: Different mouse strains infected with the same strain of Plasmodium chabaudi demonstrate remarkable variation in infection dynamics and malaria mortality.
source: Even in experimental rodent malaria infections, where environment, diet, and as many other factors as possible are highly controlled, different mouse strains infected with the same strain of Plasmodium chabaudi demonstrate remarkable variation in infection dynamics and malaria mortality.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: A mathematical model fitted to longitudinal data can predict particular functional mechanisms that lead to divergent infection dynamics.
source: Furthermore, a mathematical model fitted to these data can predict particular functional mechanisms (e.g. parasite proliferation [Mideo et al., 2011], specific versus non-specific immunity [Wale et al., 2019] and dose-dependent host responses [Haydon et al., 2003; Metcalf et al., 2011; Kamiya et al., 2020]) that lead to divergent infection dynamics (Mideo et al., 2008a; Metcalf et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous modeling studies that have demonstrated this capability.

claim: Model predictions of host immune responses against malaria are rarely examined together with immunological data.
source: Crucially, however, model predictions of host immune responses against malaria are rarely examined together with immunological data.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: It remains unclear whether and how modelled responses at the level of within-host ecology are linked to observable quantities at the cellular and molecular levels.
source: Thus, it remains unclear whether and how modelled responses at the level of within-host ecology (e.g. rate of parasite clearance) are linked to observable quantities at the cellular and molecular levels (e.g. cytokines).
evidence: This is an inference about a knowledge gap in the field based on the previous statement.

claim: The immune system is a critical proximate mechanism of host genetic resilience to infection.
source: The immune system is a critical proximate mechanism of host genetic resilience to infection (López et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to López et al., 2010.

claim: Failure to mount a robust immune response can lead to unchecked parasite proliferation.
source: Failure to mount a robust immune response can lead to unchecked parasite proliferation, while dysregulated responses may cause collateral damage, that is, immunopathology.
evidence: This is a statement based on established immunological knowledge.

claim: Dysregulated immune responses may cause collateral damage (immunopathology).
source: Failure to mount a robust immune response can lead to unchecked parasite proliferation, while dysregulated responses may cause collateral damage, that is, immunopathology.
evidence: This is a statement based on established immunological knowledge.

claim: Severe outcomes of many infectious diseases are a consequence of immunopathology rather than direct damage caused by parasites.
source: While the benefit of immune protection often outweighs any costs associated with these responses (Sorci et al., 2017), severe outcomes of many infectious diseases are a consequence of immunopathology rather than direct damage caused by parasites (Graham et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Graham et al., 2005.

claim: A 'healthy' immune response requires striking a delicate balance.
source: Thus, a 'healthy' immune response requires striking a delicate balance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the previous statements about immune responses.

claim: During the acute phase of blood-stage malaria infection, innate responses target and remove iRBCs as well as short-lived extracellular parasites known as merozoites.
source: During the acute phase of blood-stage malaria infection, innate responses target and remove iRBCs as well as short-lived extracellular parasites known as merozoites (Stevenson and Riley, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stevenson and Riley, 2004.

claim: RBCs, regardless of infection status, are susceptible to clearance by immune effectors such as macrophages.
source: In addition, RBCs — regardless of infection status — are susceptible to clearance by immune effectors such as macrophages (Jakeman et al., 1999; Chua et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jakeman et al., 1999 and Chua et al., 2013.

claim: Data-driven modelling studies highlight the importance of indiscriminate RBC clearance for lowering parasite burden.
source: While the targeted response removes more iRBCs, data-driven modelling studies highlight the importance of indiscriminate RBC clearance for lowering parasite burden (Wale et al., 2019; Kamiya et al., 2020; Metcalf et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple modeling studies.

claim: Host-driven destruction of RBCs has been proposed as a host adaptation to clear parasites directly (top-down effect) and to limit resources for the parasite (bottom-up effect).
source: On the one hand, it has been proposed as a host adaptation in the presence of malaria parasites to clear the parasites directly (i.e. top-down effect) as well as to limit resources for the parasite (i.e. bottom-up effect) (Wale et al., 2019; Haydon et al., 2003; Metcalf et al., 2012; Cromer et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies proposing this mechanism.

claim: An excessive loss of RBCs brings forth adverse health implications.
source: On the other hand, an excessive loss of RBCs brings forth adverse health implications.
evidence: This is a statement based on established medical knowledge.

claim: In immune naive infants and children, severe malarial anaemia is the most common severe manifestation of disease.
source: In immune naive infants and children, severe malarial anaemia is the most common severe manifestation of disease, and its associated mortality rate can reach 30% (Perkins et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Perkins et al., 2011.

claim: The mortality rate associated with severe malarial anaemia can reach 30%.
source: In immune naive infants and children, severe malarial anaemia is the most common severe manifestation of disease, and its associated mortality rate can reach 30% (Perkins et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Perkins et al., 2011.

claim: Clearance is the most important process causing malaria-related anaemia, accounting for between 75% and 90% of the total RBC deficit during malaria infections.
source: Among them, clearance is the most important process, accounting for between 75% and 90% of the total RBC deficit during malaria infections (Jakeman et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jakeman et al., 1999.

claim: Direct exploitation by malaria parasites accounts for less than 10% of the RBC deficit.
source: In comparison, direct exploitation by malaria parasites has been estimated to account for less than 10% of the RBC deficit (Jakeman et al., 1999; Price et al., 2001; Fonseca et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: Vertebrate host responses are regulated by immune signalling molecules known as cytokines.
source: At the molecular level, vertebrate host responses are regulated by immune signalling molecules, known as cytokines (Lamb et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lamb et al., 2006.

claim: Acute malaria infection induces pro-inflammatory cytokines required for mounting a timely and robust response.
source: Acute malaria infection induces pro-inflammatory cytokines required for mounting a timely and robust response while anti-inflammatory cytokines inhibit excess immune reactions to safeguard against collateral damage (Lamb et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lamb et al., 2006.

claim: Anti-inflammatory cytokines inhibit excess immune reactions to safeguard against collateral damage.
source: Acute malaria infection induces pro-inflammatory cytokines required for mounting a timely and robust response while anti-inflammatory cytokines inhibit excess immune reactions to safeguard against collateral damage (Lamb et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lamb et al., 2006.

claim: Inflammatory responses can be damaging to the organisms that produce them.
source: However, the same inflammatory responses can also be damaging to the organisms that produce them (Clark et al., 1991; King and Lamb, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clark et al., 1991 and King and Lamb, 2015.

claim: TNF-α overproduction could lead to adverse effects including worsened anaemia, weight loss and survival in the mouse model.
source: For example, TNF-α overproduction — which can result from a deficit of anti-inflammatory cytokines like interleukin 10 (IL-10) and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) — could lead to adverse effects including worsened anaemia, weight loss and survival in the mouse model (Omer and Riley, 1998; Li et al., 2003; Long et al., 2006; Long et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: TNF-α overproduction can result from a deficit of anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10 and TGF-β.
source: For example, TNF-α overproduction — which can result from a deficit of anti-inflammatory cytokines like interleukin 10 (IL-10) and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) — could lead to adverse effects including worsened anaemia, weight loss and survival in the mouse model (Omer and Riley, 1998; Li et al., 2003; Long et al., 2006; Long et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Balanced expression of cytokines is likely a mechanism that promotes resilience (survival) to malaria infection.
source: Balanced expression of these cytokines is likely a mechanism that promotes resilience (survival) to malaria infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the previous discussion of cytokine effects.

claim: Mechanistic studies usually focus on just one or two inbred mouse strains with similar cytokine responses, limiting our ability to link molecular signatures with functional variation in host traits.
source: However, mechanistic studies usually focus on just one or two inbred mouse strains with similar cytokine responses, limiting our ability to link molecular signatures with functional variation in host traits (e.g. indiscriminate versus targeted RBC clearance) that impacts the infection dynamics.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current research approaches based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: The mathematical model of within-host malaria ecology accurately described the time-course of RBCs and iRBCs during the acute phase of malaria infection in all mouse strains.
source: Our mathematical model of within-host malaria infection accurately described the time-course of RBCs and iRBCs during the acute phase of malaria infection in all mouse strains (Appendices 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to model fitting results in Appendices 1 and 2.

claim: Several estimated model parameters varied with mouse strain.
source: Several estimated model parameters varied with mouse strain (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4, which shows parameter variation.

claim: There is a general negative association between β and host survival.
source: While we found a general negative association between β and host survival (Figure 4) — with a notable exception of PWK/PhJ mice — little is documented on the host's contribution to variation in iRBC burst size.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The flow cytometry marker TER119 works poorly with WSB/EiJ.
source: For example, the flow cytometry marker, TER119, a standard marker for mouse erythroid cells, works poorly with WSB/EiJ, hinting at a possible difference in RBC surface proteins (Davis, personal observation).
evidence: The claim is based on a personal observation by Davis.

claim: WSB/EiJ maintained comparatively much lower iRBC densities.
source: Overall, WSB/EiJ excelled in every facet of resilience against P. chabaudi AJ and maintained comparatively much lower iRBC densities (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Infection resilience in WSB/EiJ may generalise to other malaria parasites, including P. berghei.
source: Infection resilience in this mouse strain may generalise to other malaria parasites, including P. berghei (Bopp et al., 2010), yet interestingly, these mice are highly vulnerable to Salmonella infections (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bopp et al., 2010.

claim: WSB/EiJ mice are highly vulnerable to Salmonella infections.
source: Infection resilience in this mouse strain may generalise to other malaria parasites, including P. berghei (Bopp et al., 2010), yet interestingly, these mice are highly vulnerable to Salmonella infections (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Three less resilient strains (CAST/EiJ, NOD/ShiLtJ, and PWK/PhJ) clustered together in the PCA biplot, indicating their functional similarity.
source: Three less resilient strains (CAST/EiJ, NOD/ShiLtJ, and PWK/PhJ) clustered together in the PCA biplot (Figure 5), indicating their functional similarity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: General RBC clearance is likely harmful in A/J mice.
source: Given the poor resilience of these mice (20% survival; Figure 1), general RBC clearance is likely harmful, at least in this strain of mice.
evidence: This is an inference from the combination of high indiscriminate clearance and poor survival.

claim: The 'scorched-earth tactic' could remove healthy RBCs in excess and trigger severe anaemia that causes host mortality.
source: While the host potentially stands to benefit from destroying RBCs by removing some iRBCs and taking the resource away from malaria parasites, this 'scorched-earth tactic' (Wale et al., 2019) could remove healthy RBCs in excess and trigger severe anaemia that causes host mortality.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential negative consequences of indiscriminate RBC clearance.

claim: The significant role of indiscriminate RBC clearance on severe anaemia is empirically supported by a study that demonstrated a high turnover of transfused RBCs in BALB/c mice infected with P. berghei.
source: The significant role of indiscriminate RBC clearance on severe anaemia is empirically supported by a study that demonstrated a high turnover of transfused RBCs in BALB/c mice infected with P. berghei (Evans et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Evans et al., 2006.

claim: The clearance of transfused RBCs was likely immune-mediated as severe anaemia was alleviated by depletion of immune cells.
source: The clearance was likely immune-mediated as severe anaemia was alleviated by depletion of immune cells (Evans et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Evans et al., 2006.

claim: A/J mice are defective in the production of new RBCs during malaria infection.
source: Another study observed lower young RBC (i.e., reticulocyte) counts in A/J mice and postulated that these mice are defective in the production of new RBCs during malaria infection (Chang et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chang et al., 2004.

claim: Among poorly resilient strains, A/J mice showed the lowest propensity to upregulate erythropoiesis.
source: This is consistent with our model prediction that, among poorly resilient strains, A/J mice showed the lowest propensity to upregulate erythropoiesis (lower ρ values, relative to CAST/EiJ, NOD/ShiLtJ, and PWK/PhJ; Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The lower ρ values in A/J mice may reflect the inhibitory effect of inflammation on the steady-state erythropoiesis that takes place in the bone marrow.
source: Together with our finding that A/J mice mount a stronger response than other poorly resilient strains (Figure 4), the lower ρ values in A/J mice may reflect the inhibitory effect of inflammation on the steady-state erythropoiesis that takes place in the bone marrow (Morceau et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on model results and a citation to Morceau et al., 2009.

claim: Inflammatory responses induce stress erythropoiesis in the spleen.
source: As the interactions between inflammation and erythropoiesis are complex (e.g., inflammatory responses also induce stress erythropoiesis in the spleen [Paulson et al., 2020] and erythropoietin [EPO, cytokine primarily responsible for RBC production] inhibits inflammation [Nairz et al., 2012]), further investigation is needed to better understand the net impact of malaria-induced immune responses on RBC production.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Paulson et al., 2020.

claim: Erythropoietin inhibits inflammation.
source: As the interactions between inflammation and erythropoiesis are complex (e.g., inflammatory responses also induce stress erythropoiesis in the spleen [Paulson et al., 2020] and erythropoietin [EPO, cytokine primarily responsible for RBC production] inhibits inflammation [Nairz et al., 2012]), further investigation is needed to better understand the net impact of malaria-induced immune responses on RBC production.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nairz et al., 2012.

claim: Blood transfusion or EPO injection to replenish depleted RBCs in severe anaemia may be most effective against patients that are particularly prone to indiscriminate RBC clearance.
source: First, blood transfusion or EPO injection to replenish depleted RBCs in severe anaemia may be most effective against patients that are particularly prone to indiscriminate RBC clearance.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about clinical implications based on the model results.

claim: Timely EPO injection alleviates anaemia and improves survival in A/J mice.
source: In fact, timely EPO injection alleviates anaemia and improves survival in A/J mice (Chang et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chang et al., 2004.

claim: EPO treatment may be less effective against poorly resilient patients whose mortality is attributed to insufficient immune responses.
source: However, the same treatment may be less effective against other poorly resilient patients (similar to CAST/EiJ, NOD/ShiLtJ, and PWK/PhJ) whose mortality is attributed to insufficient immune responses (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about clinical implications based on the model results.

claim: The possibility of immunopathology has been largely overlooked in the vaccine development process.
source: Alarmingly, the possibility of immunopathology has so far been largely overlooked in the vaccine development process (Stanisic and Good, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stanisic and Good, 2016.

claim: Poor survival was associated with hosts with the weakest activation of the targeted response (in CAST/EiJ, NOD/ShiLtJ and PWK/PhJ), or the strongest activation of the indiscriminate response (in A/J).
source: In summary, our model predicted that poor survival was associated with hosts with the weakest activation of the targeted response (in CAST/EiJ, NOD/ShiLtJ and PWK/PhJ), or the strongest activation of the indiscriminate response (in A/J).
evidence: This is a summary of the model predictions based on the data analysis.

claim: The host's ability to mount a precise response to clear parasites is likely a major determinant of host survival.
source: Thus, the host's ability to mount a precise response to clear parasites is likely a major determinant of host survival.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model predictions.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IFN-γ impact malaria parasite clearance.
source: Notably, pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IFN-γ impact malaria parasite clearance, while anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10 and TGF-β are crucial for limiting inflammation and immunopathology (Artavanis-Tsakonas et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Artavanis-Tsakonas et al., 2003.

claim: Anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10 and TGF-β are crucial for limiting inflammation and immunopathology.
source: Notably, pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IFN-γ impact malaria parasite clearance, while anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10 and TGF-β are crucial for limiting inflammation and immunopathology (Artavanis-Tsakonas et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Artavanis-Tsakonas et al., 2003.

claim: Resilient strains (WSB/EiJ, 129S1/SvImJ, NZO/HILtJ, C57BL/6) showed a higher level of cytokine activity (both pro- and anti-inflammatory).
source: In general, resilient strains (WSB/EiJ, 129S1/SvImJ, NZO/HILtJ, C57BL/6) showed a higher level of cytokine activity (both pro- and anti-inflammatory; Figure 6a,b and c) while poorly resilient strains showed either a relatively stunted activity (CAST/EiJ and PWK/PhJ), or tendency towards pro-inflammatory biased expression (NOD/ShiLtJ and A/J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Poorly resilient strains showed either a relatively stunted cytokine activity (CAST/EiJ and PWK/PhJ), or tendency towards pro-inflammatory biased expression (NOD/ShiLtJ and A/J).
source: In general, resilient strains (WSB/EiJ, 129S1/SvImJ, NZO/HILtJ, C57BL/6) showed a higher level of cytokine activity (both pro- and anti-inflammatory; Figure 6a,b and c) while poorly resilient strains showed either a relatively stunted activity (CAST/EiJ and PWK/PhJ), or tendency towards pro-inflammatory biased expression (NOD/ShiLtJ and A/J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The model predicted that highly resilient mouse strains 129S1/SvImJ, NZO/HILtJ and C57BL/6 activate the targeted response more strongly than the less resilient CAST/EiJ, NOD/ShiLtJ, and PWK/PhJ.
source: Specifically, the model predicted that the highly resilient mouse strains 129S1/SvImJ, NZO/HILtJ and to a large extent C57BL/6, activate the targeted response more strongly than the less resilient CAST/EiJ, NOD/ShiLtJ, and PWK/PhJ.
evidence: This is a summary of the model predictions.

claim: The model prediction of stronger targeted response in resilient strains was consistent with the higher expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in these strains.
source: This prediction was consistent with the higher expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in these strains (Figure 6a,b and c), in comparison to two of the lesser resilient strains (CAST/EiJ and PWK/PhJ) for which we predicted weak immune responses (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is an inference linking model predictions to cytokine data.

claim: In 129S1/SvImJ, NZO/HILtJ, and C57BL/6, the robust expression of TNF-α and IFN-γ was matched by equally robust expression of IL-10 and TGF-β.
source: Importantly, in the three strains that show higher survival (129S1/SvImJ, NZO/HILtJ, and C57BL/6), the robust expression of TNF-α and IFN-γ was matched by equally robust expression of IL-10 and TGF-β (Figure 6d), which inhibit overproduction of immune effectors (Artavanis-Tsakonas et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Less resilient CAST/EiJ and PWK/PhJ showed a comparatively low expression of both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Less resilient CAST/EiJ and PWK/PhJ showed a comparatively low expression of both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines (Figure 6a,b and c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The lower pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in CAST/EiJ and PWK/PhJ draws a parallel with modelling results that these strains show comparatively weaker immune activation.
source: The lower pro-inflammatory cytokine expression draws a parallel with our modelling results that CAST/EiJ and PWK/PhJ show comparatively weaker immune activation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference linking cytokine data to model predictions.

claim: NOD/ShiLtJ and A/J showed signs of pro-inflammatory bias in cytokine expressions.
source: We found signs of pro-inflammatory bias in the cytokine expressions of NOD/ShiLtJ and A/J (Figure 6), both of which are poorly resilient at 40% and 20% survival, respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In NOD/ShiLtJ and A/J, elevated expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (particularly IFN-γ) was not matched by a corresponding increase in anti-inflammatory responses.
source: In these strains, we observed elevated expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (particularly IFN-γ) without a matched increase in anti-inflammatory responses (Figure 6b,c and d), which inhibit overproduction of immune effectors (Artavanis-Tsakonas et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Immunoregulatory imbalance is associated with immunopathology during malaria infections.
source: However, immunoregulatory imbalance is also associated with immunopathology during malaria infections (King and Lamb, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to King and Lamb, 2015.

claim: Overproduction of immune effectors could cause collateral host tissue damage and excessive indiscriminate RBC clearance may lead to severe anaemia.
source: In particular, overproduction of immune effectors could cause collateral host tissue damage and excessive indiscriminate RBC clearance may lead to severe anaemia.
evidence: This is a statement based on established immunological knowledge.

claim: Modelling results and cytokine assays together suggest a causal link between the strength of host-driven destruction of RBCs and the underlying pro-inflammatory bias.
source: Thus, our modelling results and cytokine assays together suggest a causal link between the strength of host-driven destruction of RBCs — which may be both beneficial and detrimental to the host (Wale et al., 2019; Perkins et al., 2011) — and the underlying pro-inflammatory bias (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is an inference linking model predictions to cytokine data.

claim: NOD mice are documented for immunodeficiencies downstream of inflammatory cytokines, including severely reduced natural killer cell activity.
source: However, NOD mice are documented for immunodeficiencies downstream of inflammatory cytokines: for example, severely reduced natural killer cell activity (Kataoka et al., 1983), hyporesponsiveness of macrophages to growth factors and IFN-γ (Serreze et al., 1993), and defective development of antigen-presenting dendritic cells (Pearson et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kataoka et al., 1983.

claim: NOD mice show hyporesponsiveness of macrophages to growth factors and IFN-γ.
source: However, NOD mice are documented for immunodeficiencies downstream of inflammatory cytokines: for example, severely reduced natural killer cell activity (Kataoka et al., 1983), hyporesponsiveness of macrophages to growth factors and IFN-γ (Serreze et al., 1993), and defective development of antigen-presenting dendritic cells (Pearson et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Serreze et al., 1993.

claim: NOD mice show defective development of antigen-presenting dendritic cells.
source: However, NOD mice are documented for immunodeficiencies downstream of inflammatory cytokines: for example, severely reduced natural killer cell activity (Kataoka et al., 1983), hyporesponsiveness of macrophages to growth factors and IFN-γ (Serreze et al., 1993), and defective development of antigen-presenting dendritic cells (Pearson et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pearson et al., 2003.

claim: Model prediction and cytokine assay together indicate that inflammatory responses at the molecular level failed to translate functionally to effective clearance of malaria parasites in NOD/ShiLtJ.
source: Thus, our model prediction and cytokine assay together indicate that inflammatory responses at the molecular level failed to translate functionally to effective clearance of malaria parasites.
evidence: This is an inference linking model predictions, cytokine data, and known immunodeficiencies in NOD mice.

claim: WSB/EiJ mice experience exceptionally low iRBC density.
source: However, it is worth highlighting that the WSB/EiJ mice experience exceptionally low iRBC density (Figure 2) and hence the cue for triggering cytokine production remains low.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When scaled by iRBC density, the propensity of WSB/EiJ to express both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines generally exceeds that of other resilient strains.
source: When scaled by the iRBC density, it becomes apparent that the propensity of WSB/EiJ to express both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines generally exceeds that of other resilient strains (Figure 6d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Cytokine assays complemented mathematical modelling by uncovering variation in molecular mechanisms that underlies functional differences among host strains that show diverse infection outcomes.
source: Overall, cytokine assays complemented mathematical modelling by uncovering variation in molecular mechanisms that underlies functional differences among host strains that show diverse infection outcomes.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the integration of modeling and cytokine data.

claim: Host resilience to Plasmodium infection was linked to a balanced expression of pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Host resilience to Plasmodium infection was linked to a balanced expression of pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the cytokine data and survival outcomes.

claim: Poorly resilient strains either showed stunted activation of pro-inflammatory cytokines associated with insufficient parasite control, or pro-inflammatory bias that has been implicated in immunopathology.
source: Poorly resilient strains either showed stunted activation of pro-inflammatory cytokines associated with insufficient parasite control, or pro-inflammatory bias that has been implicated in immunopathology (Artavanis-Tsakonas et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a summary inference from the cytokine data and survival outcomes, supported by a citation.

claim: Immune responses are a key host factor influencing protection from malaria infections.
source: It is well documented that immune responses are a key host factor influencing protection from malaria infections (López et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to López et al., 2010.

claim: It remains difficult to relate health outcomes to the underlying variation in host immunity because parasite load, immune regulation and host health are intertwined and are variable over time.
source: However, it remains difficult to relate health outcomes to the underlying variation in host immunity because parasite load, immune regulation and host health are intertwined and are variable over time.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in the field based on the authors' assessment.

claim: A knowledge gap exists between what is empirically measurable at the molecular and cellular level to what is functionally important to infection dynamics at the within-host ecological level.
source: However, a knowledge gap exists between what is empirically measurable (at the molecular and cellular level, for example immune molecules and cells) to what is functionally important to infection dynamics (at the within-host ecological level, for example net effect of parasite clearance).
evidence: This is a statement about a knowledge gap in the field based on the authors' assessment.

claim: Better host survival during malaria infection was associated with precisely targeted, robust clearance of blood-stage parasites.
source: At the within-host ecological level, our dynamical modelling of infection revealed that better host survival during malaria infection was associated with precisely targeted, robust clearance of blood-stage parasites.
evidence: This is a summary of the model predictions based on the data analysis.

claim: Well-regulated inflammatory cytokine expressions are key molecular signatures of inbred mouse strains that survive malaria infections.
source: Using cross-sectional cytokine assays, we uncovered well-regulated inflammatory cytokine expressions are key molecular signatures of inbred mouse strains that survive malaria infections.
evidence: This is a summary of the cytokine assay findings.

claim: By augmenting mathematical modelling of within-host ecology with cross-sectional cytokine assays, the study narrows the gap between functional and molecular mechanisms of host resilience to malaria infection.
source: By augmenting mathematical modelling of within-host ecology with cross-sectional cytokine assays, our study narrows the gap between functional and molecular mechanisms of host resilience to malaria infection.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the study.

claim: Mice were administered the AJ strain of Plasmodium chabaudi at a dose of 10^5 iRBCs.
source: We administered the AJ strain of Plasmodium chabaudi to the experimental animals at a dose of 105 iRBCs and monitored infections longitudinally, for 15 days, as previously described (Torres et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Infections were monitored longitudinally for 15 days.

claim: High host mortality was associated with either weak parasite clearance, or a strong, yet imprecise response that inadvertently removes uninfected cells in excess.
